title: Chinese Prosecutors' Paper Floats Treating Mixer, Privacy-Coin Use as Laundering Signal
dek: An article in China's top prosecutors' paper urges new blockchain evidence rules and presumptions of laundering intent tied to mixer and privacy-coin use. It also proposes a state platform to sell seized coins.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: The article proposes presumptions of intent for mixer and privacy-coin use, plus a state platform to sell seized coins.
bottom_line: Watch whether China's banking regulator or Ministry of Justice formally adopts or comments on the presumption framework. If formal rulemaking follows, the precedent could pressure other jurisdictions to define privacy-tool use as suspicious, creating global compliance friction for users who employ mixers or privacy coins for legitimate purposes.
body: An article published in China's top prosecutors' official paper has proposed new blockchain evidence rules that would treat the use of cryptocurrency mixers and privacy coins as a legal presumption of money-laundering intent, according to Decrypt's reporting. The proposal also includes establishing a state platform to sell seized cryptocurrency.

The framework would shift the evidentiary burden: instead of requiring prosecutors to prove intent to launder, the mere use of privacy-enhancing tools would constitute prima facie evidence of that intent. For legitimate users of privacy tools, the proposal raises compliance risk; a tool choice alone could trigger investigative action or seizure without proof of underlying criminal conduct.

The proposal also calls for new blockchain evidence rules to support enforcement. Per Decrypt, the prosecutors' paper suggests creating a state-managed platform specifically to auction digital assets seized in enforcement actions, establishing infrastructure for handling cryptocurrency forfeitures.

The articles and proposals remain in the prosecutors' publication and have not, according to available reporting, been endorsed by a formal regulatory body or government ministry. Whether the proposals will move to formal regulation or legislation, and what timeline such movement might follow, remains unclear.
